enhanced.fullText:
The Copyright Term Extension Act of 1998, codified in 17 U.S.C. § 302-304, significantly extended copyright protection periods in the United States, directly impacting higher education institutions' use of copyrighted materials for research, teaching, and scholarship. This federal legislation, also known as the Sonny Bono Act, added 20 years to existing copyright terms across all categories of protected works.

Under 17 U.S.C. § 302(a), works created after January 1, 1978, now receive protection for the life of the author plus 70 years, extended from the previous 50-year post-mortem term. For works made for hire, anonymous works, and pseudonymous works under 17 U.S.C. § 302(c), protection extends to 95 years from first publication or 120 years from creation, whichever is shorter.

The Act establishes specific provisions in 17 U.S.C. § 108(h) creating limited exemptions for qualifying educational institutions. Libraries, archives, and nonprofit educational institutions may treat works in their final 20 years of copyright protection as if they were in the public domain for preservation, scholarship, or research purposes, provided three critical conditions are met: (1) good faith determination that the work is not subject to normal commercial exploitation; (2) verification that copies cannot be obtained at reasonable prices; and (3) immediate cessation of use upon copyright owner notification.

Higher education institutions must implement comprehensive copyright compliance programs addressing fair use analysis under 17 U.S.C. § 107, particularly for course reserves, digital collections, and distance learning materials. The Digital Millennium Copyright Act's safe harbor provisions in 17 U.S.C. § 512 require institutions to designate copyright agents and implement takedown procedures.

Violations can result in statutory damages ranging from $750 to $30,000 per work under 17 U.S.C. § 504(c), with willful infringement potentially reaching $150,000 per work. Institutions face additional exposure through vicarious and contributory liability theories when faculty or students engage in infringing activities using institutional resources.

Compliance requires ongoing assessment of institutional policies, faculty training programs, and systematic review of digital repositories and course materials to ensure adherence to extended copyright terms and proper application of educational exemptions.
enhanced.summary: The Copyright Term Extension Act extends copyright protection by 20 years, requiring higher education institutions to reassess fair use policies, implement robust compliance programs, and utilize the limited educational exemption for preservation and research activities during works' final 20-year protection period.
enhanced.requirements:
## Core Copyright Compliance
- Establish institutional copyright policies addressing extended 70-year post-mortem and 95-year work-for-hire terms under 17 U.S.C. § 302
- Designate qualified copyright compliance officers with legal training
- Implement systematic review processes for course materials and digital collections

## Educational Exemption Implementation
- Document good faith investigations of commercial availability per 17 U.S.C. § 108(h)
- Establish reasonable price determination procedures for scholarly works
- Create notification systems for immediate cessation upon copyright owner objection

## Faculty and Staff Training
- Conduct annual copyright training covering extended terms and fair use analysis
- Provide guidance on DMCA safe harbor compliance under 17 U.S.C. § 512
- Develop clear protocols for course reserves and distance learning materials

## Risk Management Procedures
- Maintain comprehensive documentation of copyright decisions and fair use analyses
- Establish legal review processes for high-risk uses and institutional repositories
enhanced.reportingRequirements: No direct federal reporting requirements exist under the Copyright Term Extension Act. However, institutions must maintain detailed records of copyright compliance decisions, fair use analyses, and educational exemption usage. DMCA takedown notices and responses must be documented per 17 U.S.C. § 512 safe harbor requirements.
